title: Sri Rag
hook: the first raga (ang 14), serious and grand, often linked with evening

segments.voice: Yesterday, the order of the ragas, Sri to Jaijavanti, and your line was thirty-one moods. Today, the first name on that list.

The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't open with a raga section. It opens with the Japji, which carries no raga in its heading, and then a short set of hymns for evening and night. Only after those, on ang fourteen, does the first of the long raga sections begin. Its name is short, and it sounds like a title of honor: Sri. The music of the book's main body starts here.
screen: `FIRST, THE JAPJI.` → `THEN A SHORT SET OF HYMNS.` → `THEN, ON ANG 14: SRI RAG.`

segments.voice: What does Sri Rag sound like? In the Indian musical tradition it's heard as weighty and grand, a raga of dignity more than sparkle, and tradition places it in the evening, as the light goes. Slow phrases, low notes, a melody that won't be hurried: the sound of someone sitting down to say something serious. The Gurus put a great deal of serious speech into it. Earlier on the path you met two of its hymns, the river and the fish, and the four watches of the night. Sri Rag holds the voices of more than one Guru, and of Bhagats after them. The Granth even comments on this raga by name. In a salok in Sri Rag's own var, Guru Amar Das says, in paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag is the best, if through it a person holds love for the True One. Then, he goes on, the True Lord lives in the mind always, and the understanding becomes steady and boundless. Listen to the shape of that. The praise comes with an if. The raga isn't holy just for standing first in the book; it's worth what it leads to. And what it leads to is steadiness, a mind that doesn't lurch. A slow, grave, evening raga, and a promise of a steady mind: the sound and the meaning point the same way. So when kirtan is sung in Sri Rag, the music asks the listener to slow down before the words even arrive. Tomorrow, one of its hymns, sung through a whole night.
screen: `WEIGHTY, GRAND, AN EVENING RAGA.` · `THE RIVER, THE FISH, THE WATCHES.` · `THE BEST, IF IT BRINGS LOVE OF THE TRUE ONE.` · then, large: `THE FIRST RAGA.`

segments.voice: Play a shabad sung in Sri Rag, or the raga on an instrument, and follow the pace before the words, letting your breathing slow to meet it. If you can't find one, sit facing a window, watch the light wherever it is in its day, and breathe at the speed of a slow song. If you pray, say Waheguru once, as slowly as the raga would.
Sri Rag. The first raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib, heard as grave and grand, placed by tradition in the evening, and praised by Guru Amar Das if it brings love of the True One. Today's word.
Your line: the first raga. Grave and slow, and best when it brings love of the True One. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Is Sri Rag holy just because it comes first in the Granth?
options: No. Guru Amar Das calls it best only if through it a person holds love for the True One.
Yes. Standing first makes it the holiest raga, whoever sings it and however.
No. It's first only because it was the easiest raga for new singers to learn.

notes: 'Best' is the salok's own claim (Ang 83), paraphrased with its condition; confirm the paraphrase of the second line (the True Lord dwells in the mind; the understanding becomes steady and boundless).
The Ang 83 line was also used on day 105 (y1); here it carries the day's angle (the 'if' and steadiness).
'Heard as weighty and grand' and 'placed in the evening' are musical tradition, not stated in the Granth; framed as tradition.

The short set of hymns before Sri Rag (So Dar/Rahras and Sohila, Ang 8–13) carry their own raga headings; the hook says the Japji carries no raga and that the long raga sections begin at Ang 14, which should be accurate; confirm.
'Sounds like a title of honor' describes Sri as an honorific without giving an etymology; confirm it's acceptable.
